title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough — batching & KV cache (cost model) with Aurora Finance
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Aurora Finance through Optimize recommendations focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache. Discussed cost model assumptions, hit-rate scenarios, and tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated deployments. Agreed on a pilot benchmark and follow-up security review.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Samantha Lee (Aurora - Head of ML), Derek Wu (Aurora - Platform Eng), Nina Patel (Aurora - CTO)
Notes/links: Deck: https://redwood.gdocs/optimize-aurora-deck, Benchmark sheet: https://sheets.example.com/aurora-benchmarks

[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro, i'm Alex, AE on Redwood, with Priya our SE who will run through the Optimize walkthrough today. Sam, Derek, Nina, thanks for making time.
[00:00:12] Samantha: Hey Alex, thanks, excited to dig in. We're mainly here to understand how batching and the prefix / KV cache can help our cost numbers — we're running a user-facing chat assistant with ~6k DAU.
[00:00:28] Priya: Great, quick agenda: batching basics, KV/prefix cache, how we model hit rates into cost, deployment tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated), and next steps — open for questions anytime.
[00:00:45] Derek: Quick ask — we care about 99th p99 latency under 300ms for short queries, and cost per 1k messages needs to be within our current budget.
[00:00:58] Priya: noted, we'll point out latency tradeoffs when we discuss batch windows and caching.

[00:02:10] Priya: Ok slide 1 — batching. At a high level batching aggregates tokens across concurrent requests to amortize GPU kernel overhead. For autoregressive workloads batching typically helps throughput and lowers per-token cost but can increase tail latency depending on batch formation strategy.
[00:02:35] Alex: Two modes we recommend: latency-first (small batch sizes, continuous batching with immediate flush thresholds) and throughput-first (larger batch caps and short micro-batching windows). In Optimize we suggest heuristics based on your request qps and latencies.
[00:03:01] Samantha: What's the typical batch size you see for a chat workload like ours?
[00:03:08] Priya: For 6k DAU with average concurrency around 40-80 reqs, you might see effective batch sizes of 8-32 tokens depending on prompt lengths. But crucially, prefix cache can change that effective distribution because common prefixes avoid re-computation.

[00:04:20] Priya: Prefix / KV cache section — quick primer: prefix cache stores the KV states for commonly repeated prefixes (e.g., system prompts, few-shot examples, or conversation context) so we avoid re-running the early attention layers. KV cache stores layer key/value tensors between tokens for the same session or conversational thread. Hit rate matters: 10% vs 60% hit rate changes cost projections a lot.
[00:04:55] Derek: Our assistant uses a shared system prompt + user profile metadata. Seems like many requests will share prefixes. Is that worth caching?
[00:05:05] Priya: Yes, system prompts + static scaffolding are ideal for prefix cache. We showed in the deck an example where 40% prefix hit reduces total GPU token compute by ~25% — though this depends on model architecture and sequence length.

[00:06:30] Priya: Now the cost model slide — we build a per-token cost model combining: model cost per token (gpu-ms), batching efficiency factor, cache hit rate multiplier, and infra overheads. Example inputs in the benchmark sheet: base tokens per request, avg response length, expected cache hit rate, batch size distribution, price per GPU-hour.
[00:07:02] Alex: Important to call out assumptions: cost model assumes KV cache read/write overhead is minimal vs full forward pass for early layers, but cache eviction and sharding across pods introduces some network overhead. We include a 5-10% overhead estimate in the model.
[00:07:25] Samantha: How sensitive is the model to hit rate? If our hit rate falls from 50% to 20% what happens?
[00:07:33] Priya: In our sheet we have a scenario table — at 50% hit you might see up to 30% cost savings vs no cache; at 20% it's more like 8-12% depending on batch gains. So caching pays off more when you can keep prefixes consistent.

[00:09:00] Derek: Any gotchas around multi-tenant cache or user privacy? We can't leak a user's prefix to another user.
[00:09:09] Priya: Right — caches are sharded by customer and can be per-tenant or per-session. For PII or regulated data you'd keep KV in a private deployment or encrypted KMS-managed storage. We also maintain audit logs for cache access.
[00:09:35] Nina: Are there differences between hosted and dedicated around cache behavior?
[00:09:42] Alex: Hosted has global pooling and we can run aggressive batching and cross-tenant caching only when customers opt in; Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and more control over cache sharding and eviction policies.

[00:11:10] Priya: Demo time — i'll pull up the benchmark sheet. (screen share) Here are three scenarios: baseline (no cache, small batches), medium (prefix cache 40% hit, moderate batch window 25ms), and optimized (prefix cache 60% + larger batch caps). Note cost per million tokens drops in the optimized scenario but p99 latency rises slightly for cold requests.
[00:11:42] Samantha: Can you show absolute numbers for our workload?
[00:11:45] Priya: Sure — using your inputs (6k DAU, avg 2 messages per session, median prompt 120 tokens, response 80 tokens) baseline cost = ~$1.20 per 1k requests, medium = ~$0.85 per 1k, optimized = ~$0.62 per 1k. These are illustrative and depend on model size and quantization.
[00:12:10] Derek: That delta is attractive. What about p99 under optimized?
[00:12:15] Priya: Optimized p99 for a cold session (no prefix hit) might be 420-480ms in our sample; warm sessions (cache hit) are sub-200ms. So you get mixed outcomes.

[00:13:50] Priya: A note about quantization — 4-bit/8-bit quantized kernels reduce memory/throughput footprint and lower cost per token. However accuracy regressions vary per model, so we recommend eval sets and can help run A/Bs.
[00:14:15] Samantha: We're using an open model right now; are there model-specific recommendations?
[00:14:22] Priya: Yes — transformer variants and attention patterns affect cache locality and kernel choices. In Optimize we maintain profiles per model family (Llama-like vs Mistral-like) and recommend batch caps and KV encoding. We'll share the model profile for your model in the benchmark sheet.

[00:16:00] Derek: On infra — how do you handle eviction and state size? We'll have 100k+ active conversation contexts over time.
[00:16:10] Priya: We shard caches by conversation TTL and LRU eviction; hot shards get pinned. For very large active sets we'd suggest hybrid approach: prefix cache for system/static parts and a compressed KV for active sessions with fallback to quick recompute. Also recommend TTL pruning and TTL-based cost controls in Redwood Console.

[00:18:22] Alex: Let's quickly talk SLA and security — Aurora mentioned SOC 2 and SSO. We are SOC 2 compliant, support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC peering.
[00:18:45] Nina: We'll need an architecture diagram for the private deployment and KMS flow. Can you share that?
[00:18:50] Alex: Yes, we'll include the architecture and network diagram in the security packet; I'll put it in the follow-up email.

[00:20:05] Priya: Back to cost modeling — here's the sensitivity chart showing cost vs hit rate and avg batch latency. Small changes in hit rate produce non-linear cost reductions because batching efficiency compounds with cache savings.
[00:20:36] Samantha: Do you have recommended instrumentation for us to measure hit-rate and batch stats?
[00:20:42] Priya: Redwood Console exposes per-route cache hit metric, batch size distribution, token-ms, and cost per route. We can also ship a small instrumentation library to annotate prompts to compute prefix-keys consistently.

[00:22:10] Derek: For the pilot, we'd like to run a 2-week benchmark on Dedicated with a production-like traffic replay. Can Redwood run that or do we need to set it up?
[00:22:20] Alex: We can run a co-managed pilot — Redwood SE will run the benchmark in our sandbox dedicated pool using a sanitized trace you provide or via a replay method. We'll produce the same benchmark sheet with measured numbers.
[00:22:36] Priya: We'll need a sample trace, preferred model + checkpoint, and your success metrics (cost target, latency SLOs).

[00:24:00] Samantha: Pricing — what's the delta for Dedicated pilot? Do you require a commit?
[00:24:06] Alex: For pilots we typically offer time-boxed discounted credits; Dedicated committed pricing starts at monthly reserved capacity; we'll send detailed pricing after the call.

[00:25:30] Priya: Quick technical deep-dive: cache serialization format and network cost. We use a compressed KV layout and mandate protobufs over gRPC for inter-pod replication. Network egress for cache fetch is usually under 2% of total payload for typical models but depends on payload sizes.
[00:26:00] Derek: Any special considerations for on-prem/private?
[00:26:06] Priya: For private deployments we deploy the cache within the customer's VPC, optionally on local NVMe for fast reads. We also support encrypted KV at rest and in transit.

[00:28:12] Samantha: If we do prefix caching, how do we version prefixes when prompts change?
[00:28:20] Priya: We add prefix versioning keys into the prefix identifier; Optimize suggests a rollout where you pin a prefix version, measure hit rate, then rotate. The console shows per-prefix metrics.

[00:30:00] Alex: Let's run a quick walk-through of the benchmark sheet inputs live: (Priya types) — here's model, tokens, qps, concurrency, batch windows, prefix hit. Changing hit from 20% to 50% updates cost estimate live.
[00:30:28] Priya: Note: the sheet includes a sensitivity slider for batch window and quantization level so you can see how p99 changes.

[00:32:10] Derek: Data residency — some of our EU users' data must not leave region. Can Redwood enforce region-local caching?
[00:32:20] Alex: Yes — request routing can be regional, and cache is region-scoped for hosted. For Private we run within your region/VPC. We'll include region controls in the security doc.

[00:34:00] Samantha: We also need audit logs for cache access — can we get those forwarded to our SIEM?
[00:34:07] Alex: Yes, audit logs can be exported; we support push to common SIEMs and also provide queryable logs in Console.

[00:36:10] Priya: Ok, time to summarize what we recommend for Aurora's pilot: 1) Start with prefix caching for shared system prompts, target 40-60% expected hit, 2) run dedicated pilot with 24-72 hour production-like replay to get concrete cost numbers, 3) set batch window to latency-first initially (25ms) and then test throughput-first to see tradeoffs, 4) evaluate quantization after functional eval.
[00:36:45] Samantha: Sounds good. On metrics we'll measure cost per 1k messages, p99 latency, and hit rate.

[00:38:00] Alex: Next steps: we'll send security packet, pilot agreement, and pricing. SE to schedule benchmark kickoff after we get sanitized trace.

[00:39:10] Derek: One more technical Q — how do you handle model fallbacks if a large model isn't available in Dedicated pool?
[00:39:18] Priya: We support model variant fallbacks; Optimize can configure automatic fallback to a smaller quantized variant to preserve availability with minimal QoS impact. That also factors into the cost model as an availability tier.

[00:41:00] Priya: Quick note on observability — Console gives per-token cost, per-route latency and a diffing view for rollouts so you can catch regressions from quantization or model swaps.
[00:41:25] Samantha: We'll need that during the pilot.

[00:42:10] Alex: Recap + owners: Alex will send security packet + pricing; Priya will run the pilot benchmarks and share the filled benchmark sheet; Aurora to share sanitized trace and confirm pilot dates.

[00:42:30] Nina: We'll aim to share trace by next Tuesday.

[00:43:00] Samantha: Thanks both. Couple of typos in my notes but overall super helpful.

[00:43:15] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up with links and the pilot kickoff calendar invite.

[00:45:50] (call ends)
